title: Digital Identity for Nations: Unlinkability, Subsidiarity and Global Interoperability
description: The DPI question isn't whether identity systems harmonise across borders, but on what terms. Drawing on the digital identity research conducted with the European Decentralisation Institute earlier this year, I'll argue the credible route to global interoperability is a trust framework grounded in mutual recognition, digital subsidiarity, open standards, and constitutional change-control rather than technical centralisation; with unlinkability-by-default as a binding architectural requirement, not an add-on, and re-linking permissible only through judicial procedure. I'll ground this in evidence already in flight: Canada's Pan-Canadian Trust Framework shows federated recognition without a national identity provider; the EU–Japan Memorandum shows a transparent architecture can pull like-minded systems into alignment; Bhutan's anchoring of national identity on public Ethereum shows decentralised, privacy-preserving architecture at national scale.
